slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-two: the examination of the Tathagata.

slides.heading: Surely the Buddha is real?
points: Buddhists take refuge in him
The whole path aims at what he found
Before, during and after his life: must he exist?
slides.say: If anything is real, surely the Buddha is. Buddhists take refuge in him, and the whole path aims at what he found. So it is natural to think that whatever else turns out to be empty, the Tathagata, the one thus gone, must exist in some deeper way: before he taught, while he lived and, above all, after his death. This chapter looks for the Tathagata in the way the earlier chapters looked for a self, a mover or an agent. It does not find him there either, and it shows why that is not a loss.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Search for him in and around the five aggregates
How can a Buddha be named at all?
Is calling him 'empty' itself a view?
The nature of the Tathagata is the nature of this world
slides.say: The chapter uses the method of chapter eighteen, on the self, and of the chariot that Chandrakirti made famous: search for the person in the five aggregates and around them. It then asks how a Buddha can be named at all, whether calling him empty is itself a view, and what becomes of the old questions about the Buddha after death. It ends with one of the most quoted verses of the work: the nature of the Tathagata is the nature of this world.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: The fivefold search
slides.say: Now the explanation. The first verse is a search. A person is spoken of in dependence on the five aggregates: body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. If the Tathagata exists by his own nature, he must be findable in some relation to them. Is he the aggregates? Then he would be many, since there are five aggregates and countless moments of each, and he would arise and perish with every moment of body and mind. Is he other than the aggregates? Then he should be findable apart from them: a Tathagata with no body, no feeling, no awareness. No such being is ever met. The last three, that the aggregates are in him, that he is in them, or that he owns them, are versions of the second. A bowl holding fruit, fruit lying in a bowl, a man owning a cow: each needs two separate things. Since he is not found apart, he cannot be their container, their content or their owner. So, what here is the Tathagata? The search ends with nothing found, just as with the chariot, which is found nowhere and still carries passengers.

slides.heading: Neither own-nature nor other-nature
points: Named in dependence: no nature of his own
No borrowing from another: 'other' needs a self
Whatever depends on another is selfless
slides.say: Verses two to four take the next step. If the Buddha is named in dependence on the aggregates, he does not exist by his own nature. Could he then exist by the nature of something else, borrowing his being from the aggregates the way the moon borrows light from the sun? No. To borrow from another, there must first be someone to do the borrowing, and other only makes sense in relation to a self. One who has no own-nature has no other-nature either. Verse twenty-two point three puts it sharply: whatever exists in dependence on something else is selfless. And how could the Tathagata, the supposed deeper reality, be selfless? Nagarjuna is arguing from the opponent's own premise. For the opponent, a selfless Tathagata is no Tathagata at all. For Nagarjuna, selflessness is exactly what the Buddha taught and realised.

slides.heading: The one who takes up, and what is taken up
slides.say: Verses five to eight look at the word used for this dependence: taking up, the same word used for the fuel a fire takes up in chapter ten. So which comes first, the one who takes up, or what is taken up? If there were a Tathagata before and apart from the aggregates, he could take them up and so come to be. But there is no such Tathagata: no Buddha is ever found without body and mind. And one who does not exist before taking up cannot do the taking up. The other side fails too: nothing is taken up until it has been taken up. So taker and taken are named together, like fire and fuel, neither before the other. And the aggregates themselves are no firmer footing. They too lack own-nature. Taker and taken up are empty through and through. The opponent wanted one solid thing, at least, to which the word Tathagata could refer. There is none.

slides.heading: Not even 'empty' as a view
slides.say: Here a reader may think: then the truth about the Buddha is that he is empty. Verse twenty-two point eleven stops this at once. One should not say empty, nor not empty, nor both, nor neither. Yet these words are still spoken, for the sake of designation. This does not mean nothing can be said. Nagarjuna says empty all the time. It means that empty is not a property the Tathagata has, in the way a stone is hard. It is a word used to undo a grasp. Chapter thirteen warns that those who turn emptiness into a view are beyond help, and Chandrakirti compares emptiness to a medicine that must leave the body along with the illness it cured. Taken as the final description of what he really is, even empty would become one more elaboration.

slides.heading: The questions that do not apply
points: Permanent, impermanent, both, neither?
Does the Tathagata exist after death?
The solid grasp 'he exists' makes death look like an end
Where did the fire go? The question does not apply
slides.say: Verse twelve recalls the questions the Buddha refused to answer: whether the world is permanent, impermanent, both or neither; whether it is finite or infinite; whether the Tathagata exists after death. Nagarjuna explains the refusal. In what is at peace, empty of own-nature, there is nothing for these questions to be about. Verse thirteen shows where they come from. One who takes the solid grasp that the Tathagata exists will, on hearing of his passing, imagine that he no longer exists. Being and non-being come as a pair. Verse fourteen removes both. Since the Tathagata is empty of own-nature, the thought that after his passing he exists, or does not, has nothing to grip. This is the Buddha's answer to Vacchagotta. When a fire goes out, in which direction has it gone? The question does not apply. It asks for the whereabouts of a fire apart from its burning, and there never was such a fire.

slides.heading: Beyond elaboration
points: 'He is', 'he is not', 'he has ended'
Those who elaborate do not see the Tathagata
'Does not decay' rules out decay, not change into permanence
slides.say: Verse fifteen names the mistake behind all the questions: elaboration. The Buddha is beyond elaboration and does not decay. Those who elaborate about him, spinning out he is, he is not, he is permanent, he has ended, are struck down by their own elaborations. They do not see the Tathagata. Does not decay can sound as if the Buddha were a permanent being after all. It is not meant that way. What has no own-nature has nothing that could decay, just as it has nothing that could last. The phrase rules out decay without installing permanence. And seeing the Tathagata does not mean finding a hidden being behind the words. It means seeing as he saw: without the elaborations.

slides.heading: The nature of this world
slides.say: The chapter ends with a single verse that turns the whole search around. Whatever is the nature of the Tathagata, that is the nature of this world. The Tathagata has no nature of his own; this world has no nature of its own. This verse is easy to misread in two opposite ways. It does not say that the Buddha is just one more ordinary thing, so that awakening makes no difference. And it does not say that the world secretly contains a divine Buddha substance. It says that the Buddha and the world are empty in exactly the same way. There is no special ultimate reserved for him. The dashed box in the diagram is not a substrate under both; it marks what is not found in either. As chapter twenty-five will put it, the limit of nirvana is the limit of samsara. To see that the world has no nature of its own is to see the Tathagata.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: The Buddha still taught, and people still awaken
'Born at Lumbini' remains a true sentence
Lost: only a Buddha who exists from his own side
slides.say: The Buddha still taught; his words were heard; people still take refuge, follow the path and awaken. The Buddha was born at Lumbini and passed away at Kushinagara remains a true sentence. The name Tathagata is designated in dependence on a body, a mind, a life and its effects, and as so designated it works fully. What goes is the hope of a Buddha who exists from his own side: findable in or apart from the aggregates, surviving his death as a hidden someone or vanishing into nothing. Without that hope, the old questions are not answered but released. And reverence loses nothing. What is revered is the way of seeing that he embodied, available wherever things are seen as they are.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapter 3, the chariot and Vacchagotta
Anatta to Emptiness: The Chariot Comes Alive
The Last Refuge of Ontology; Resonances and Open Questions
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, chapter three gives Chandrakirti's sevenfold search for the chariot, the same search as the first verse here, and Vacchagotta's question about the fire that went nowhere. In The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, see The Chariot Comes Alive, on the sevenfold search; The Last Refuge of Ontology, on freedom from elaboration as the very nature of dependent arising; and Resonances and Open Questions, on ordinary experience and nirvana as equally empty. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter twenty-three, the examination of errors.
